title: Sawmills of British Columbia
hook: in the early 1900s Sikh men worked sawmills and railways on Canada's west coast

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Punjab: police in Hong Kong, railway builders in East Africa, and your line, carrying the guru abroad. Today some of those men keep going east, across the Pacific, into the forests of Canada.

Wet cedar, wood smoke, the scream of the blade: a sawmill in the rain. It's about 1906, on the coast of British Columbia. On the mill floor, among the other workers, are men in turbans, a long way from the wheat fields of Punjab. Some had heard about Canada in Hong Kong, where the ships for Vancouver set out. The pay was good, the work was hard, and the forests seemed endless.
screen: `WET CEDAR AND WOOD SMOKE.` → `TURBANS ON THE MILL FLOOR.` → `ABOUT 1906.`

segments.voice: In the first years of the 1900s, a few thousand men from Punjab, nearly all of them Sikh, arrived on Canada's west coast. They worked in sawmills and logging camps, cleared land and laid railway track. It was heavy, dangerous work, often for lower pay than other workers got. And they met hostility. Many white residents wanted Asian immigrants kept out. In 1907, British Columbia took away the vote from people of South Asian origin. From 1908, Canada required immigrants to arrive by a continuous journey from their home country, a rule almost impossible to meet from India. Immigration nearly stopped. The men already there held on. They lived together to save money, sent pay home, and built gurdwaras. In Vancouver in 1908, the Khalsa Diwan Society opened one of the first gurdwaras in North America. In 1911, Sikhs in nearby Abbotsford built one with lumber from the mills and their own hands. It still stands, the oldest surviving gurdwara in North America. A Sikh mill owner later even founded a mill town on Vancouver Island and named it Paldi, after his village in Punjab. Behind all of it is a Sikh value you already know: kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work. Guru Nanak farmed. These men milled lumber.
screen: `A FEW THOUSAND MEN FROM PUNJAB.` · `HOSTILITY, AND A CLOSED DOOR.` · `GURDWARAS BUILT FROM MILL LUMBER.` · `KIRAT KARNI: HONEST WORK.` · then, large: `HONEST WORK, FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Look around and pick one thing: the chair, the table, the walls, the paper. Somewhere, someone you'll never meet cut the tree, ran the machine, drove the truck and stacked the boards; picture their hands, and their tired evening after a long shift. If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if not, send them a silent thank you.
Kirat. Honest labor — in the early 1900s, Sikh men did it in the mills and railways of Canada's west coast, and built gurdwaras from the lumber.
Your line: honest work, far away. Mill lumber, tired hands, and the Guru close by. That's day three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, honest work, as one of the three pillars of Sikh life; in Canada, the early mill workers' gurdwaras in Vancouver and Abbotsford are remembered as the community's beginnings.
